source.title: Interpreting Neurons in Deep Vision Networks with Language Models
source.authors: Nicholas Bai; Rahul Iyer; Tuomas P. Oikarinen; Akshay R. Kulkarni; T. Weng

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates descriptions of neurons in vision networks, but does not measure any of the claim versions’ stated outcomes, such as the share of single-job neuron poles or explanations’ prediction of firing on held-out inputs.
record.gate_note: The paper’s results concern the quality and similarity of neuron descriptions. These are relevant to neuron interpretability generally, but do not measure the outcomes named in V1–V7. Its discussion of polysemantic neurons cites prior work rather than presenting a test of the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It proposes Describe-and-Dissect (DnD) for labelling vision-CNN neurons and compares its label quality against other labelling methods (human ratings, similarity to class names). It reports no share of single-job or interpretable neurons, no held-out firing prediction and no simulation scoring. It does not test the InceptionV1 cat/car neuron, attribution graphs or LLM neurons. Its mentions of polysemanticity cite Olah 2020, Mu & Andreas 2020 and Scherlis 2023 as a limitation; they are not a test. Better tools giving better labels is close to V4's mechanism, but the measure is label quality relative to other methods, not a share of interpretable neurons. So it goes under fits_no_version, not as a test of V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors also caution that human-evaluation comparisons depend on which images are shown and how, should be taken with a grain of salt, and look only at top-k activations.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops and evaluates a vision-network neuron-description pipeline using image captions, language-model summaries, and synthetic images; it does not reproduce the cited language-model neuron audit or explanation-scoring procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that probing data and how activation maps are summarized (spatial mean versus max) can change which images are selected and can affect comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: On random intermediate-layer neurons, DnD labels received higher crowd ratings than NetDissect, MILAN and CLIP-Dissect (4.15 vs 3.14–3.67 on ResNet-50; 4.14 vs 3.14–3.52 on ResNet-18). DnD labels were picked as best about 51–55% of the time. DnD labels were also closer to class names than MILAN labels on ResNet-50's final layer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-free generative neuron labelling (DnD) gives descriptions that humans rate as more accurate on top-activating images than earlier vision neuron-labelling methods.

record.problems: The main human evaluation shows only top-activating images, excludes about 25% of responses as invalid, and the authors caution that probing data, activation pooling and image display choices can affect evaluations. These description-quality results do not establish how many neurons have a single job or whether descriptions predict firing on held-out inputs.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted ablation and use-case results (including Tables 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 and 13): they concern pipeline components, pruning, or other downstream tasks and do not measure any of V1–V7. Qualitative examples were also omitted.

untested.parts: No language models of any architecture or scale.
No analysis of the InceptionV1 cat/car neuron, pose or recursive generalization.
No share of interpretable neurons by tool or architecture. No test of architecture or regularization as causes. No InceptionV1 estimates.
No attribution graphs or circuit explanations.
No test of whether labels predict firing beyond the top-k activating images. The authors only note this as a limitation of evaluation.
No simulation-based scoring of explanations on new text.

missing.what: In the scoring-function study, evaluations of neurons raters deemed uninterpretable were excluded: 276 evaluations remained from 400 (50 neurons per layer across 4 ResNet-50 layers, each rated twice). This roughly implies 69% of evaluations were on rater-judged interpretable neurons. It is a single-tool number, not a tool comparison; it is related to V4 but not a test of it.

record.verdict_notes: These are vision models (ResNet-50/18, with qualitative ViT and ResNet-152 examples), not InceptionV1 or LLMs. The pruning use case labels 'uninterpretable' neurons by how well their concepts cluster; that does not measure interpretable share. Tables 5, 8, 10, 11 and 13 are ablations or downstream comparisons and are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or their job counts.
No audit across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, or trillion-parameter scales.
No test of the InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, or recursive generalization.

The paper compares description methods on vision networks but does not estimate the share of interpretable neurons, test the proposed architecture or regularization causes, or compare architectures as the version describes.
No attribution-graph or circuit reconstruction test.
No test of whether explanations based on activating examples predict firing on held-out inputs.
No automated scoring of explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Crowdsourced rating of neuron descriptions, averaged across four intermediate layers
rows.measure: Mean human rating of description accuracy on a 1–5 scale
rows.note: Results averaged across layers; raters judged descriptions against the top 10 highly activating images.
rows.check: Rows r1–r16 compare labelling methods against each other on ratings of the top 10 images. They are not neuron-interpretability shares. About 25% of responses were excluded as invalid (1744/2400 and 443/600). The baselines are other methods, not a no-effect control.
